<!---
# Definitions

::: {#def-category}
## Category

A Category $C$ consists of the following data:

1. First class $C_0$ and another set $C_1$;

2. Functions $s, t: C_1 \rightarrow C_0$ (the source and target functions);

3. A function $\text{id} : C_0 \rightarrow C_1$ (the function which picks out an identity) such that
$\text{id}$ equalises $s$ and $t$;

4. For every $f, g \in C_1$ such that $t(f) = s(g)$ there is a unique element (there composition) $g \circ f \in C_1$ where
$s(g\circ f) = s(f)$ and $t(g \circ f) = t(g)$.

This data is required to satisfy:

For every $f \in C_1$, we have that $f \circ \text{id}(s(f)) = f$ and $\text{id}(t(f)) \circ f = f$;

For every $f, g, h \in C_1$, we have that $(h\circ g) \circ f = h \circ (g \circ f)$.
:::

:::::: {#def-double-category}
## Double Category

A [Double Category]{.underline} $\mathbb{C}$ consists of the following data:

1. a Category $\ \mathbb{C}_0 \ $, whose objects we call 0-[cells]{.underline}, and whose arrows we call [tight]{.underline} 1-[cells]{.underline}
$f: V \rightarrow V'$;

2. a Category $\ \mathbb{C}_1 \ $, whose objects we call [loose]{.underline} 1-[cells]{.underline} $M: V \not\rightarrow W$, and whose
arrows we call 2-[cells]{.underline}

::: {.imagify}
[]: %
\begin{tikzcd}
	V && W \\
	& {\Downarrow \phi} \\
	V' && W'
	\arrow["M"{inner sep=.8ex}, "\shortmid"{marking}, from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow["f"', from=1-1, to=3-1]
	\arrow["g", from=1-3, to=3-3]
	\arrow["M'"'{inner sep=.8ex}, "\shortmid"{marking}, from=3-1, to=3-3]
\end{tikzcd}
:::

3. two functors $\text{src}, \text{tgt} : \mathbb{C}_1 \rightarrow \mathbb{C}_0$ called [source]{.underline}
and [target]{.underline} respectively;


4. [composition]{.underline} and [identity]{.underline} functors $\circ : \mathbb{C}_1 \times_{\mathbb{C}_0} \mathbb{C}_1 \rightarrow \mathbb{C}_1$ and $\text{id} : \mathbb{C}_0 \rightarrow \mathbb{C}_1$;

5. natural families of isomorphisms in $\mathbb{C}_1$:

::: {.imagify}
[]: %
\begin{tikzcd}
	V && Y \\
	& {\Downarrow a_{P,N,M}} \\
	V && Y
	\arrow["(P\circ N) \circ M"{inner sep=.8ex}, "\shortmid"{marking}, from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow[equals, nfold, from=1-1, to=3-1]
	\arrow[equals, nfold, from=1-3, to=3-3]
	\arrow["P \circ (N \circ M)"'{inner sep=.8ex}, "\shortmid"{marking}, from=3-1, to=3-3]
\end{tikzcd}
:::

::: {.imagify}
[]: %
\begin{tikzcd}
	V && W \\
	& {\Downarrow \ell_M} \\
	V && W
	\arrow["\text{id}_W \circ M"{inner sep=.8ex}, "\shortmid"{marking}, from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow[equals, nfold, from=1-1, to=3-1]
	\arrow[equals, nfold, from=1-3, to=3-3]
	\arrow["M"'{inner sep=.8ex}, "\shortmid"{marking}, from=3-1, to=3-3]
\end{tikzcd}
:::

::: {.imagify}
[]: %
\begin{tikzcd}
	V && W \\
	& {\Downarrow r_M} \\
	V && W
	\arrow["M \circ \text{id}_V"{inner sep=.8ex}, "\shortmid"{marking}, from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow[equals, nfold, from=1-1, to=3-1]
	\arrow[equals, nfold, from=1-3, to=3-3]
	\arrow["M"'{inner sep=.8ex}, "\shortmid"{marking}, from=3-1, to=3-3]
\end{tikzcd}
:::

These data are required to satisfy the following coherence axioms which manifest as equations between composite 2-cells.

The first of these is the following composite,

	\arrow[equals, nfold, from=3-3, to=5-3]

	\arrow[equals, nfold, from=5-1, to=7-1]
	\arrow[equals, nfold, from=5-3, to=7-3]
	\arrow["Q \circ (P \circ (N \circ M))"'{inner sep=.8ex}, "\shortmid"{marking}, from=7-1, to=7-3]

is required to be equal to this composite,

::: {.imagify}
[]: %

	\arrow["((Q \circ P)\circ N) \circ M"{inner sep=.8ex}, "\shortmid"{marking}, from=1-1, to=1-3]

A further equation is required, which declares that the next composite

	\arrow["(M \circ \text{id}_W)\circ N"{inner sep=.8ex}, "\shortmid"{marking}, from=1-1, to=1-3]

::::::

Several questions come about when staring at the above definition. If arrows are objects in $\mathbb{C}_1$ what gives the
right to state that they look like arrows with sources and targets that could just as well be source and targets of arrows in $\mathbb{C}_0$.
The source and target functors are lacking defining equations they should be compatible with the composition and identity functors in the way
that is implied from the mantra "double categories are category objects in the category of categories". In particular, the identity functor must
equalise the source and target functors meaning that enrichment is ill-defined or based on evil equality. The more significant problem is that the
presentation of squares need to have a specific orientation which produces conflicts in the literature.

A better definition starts from finding a better definition for categories.

::: {#def-category-indexed}
## Category, indexed version

A category is the data of:

1. A class $C_0$;

2. For every $A, B \in C_0$ a set $C_1(A,B)$;

3. For every $A \in C_0$, a distinguished element $\text{id}_A \in C_1(A,A)$;

4. For every $A, B, C \in C_0$, and every $f \in C_1(A, B)$, as well as $g \in C_1(B,C)$
there is a $g \circ f \in C_1(A,C)$;

satisfying the requirements that

For every $A, B \in C_0$, and every $f \in C_1(A, B)$ the following equations hold

$$f \circ \text{id}_A = f = \text{id}_B \circ f.$$

For every $A, B, C, D \in C_0$, and every $f \in C_1(A, B)$ and also every $g \in C_1(B,C)$ as well as $h \in C_1(C, D)$,
the following equation holds

$$(h \circ g) \circ f = h \circ (g \circ f).$$

The sets $C_1(A,B)$ are pairwise disjoint.
:::

It can be shown through a laborious formal argument that the two definitions, the version with source and target and the indexed version are equivalent and thus we can
use the capitalised or uncapitalised interchangeably.
We would like to have a similar definition for double categories as for the definition of category. The reason to do this is so that there is no confusion in the definition and
data can be expressed clearly.


::: {#def-double-category-indexed}
## Double category, indexed version

A double category $\mathbb{C}$ consists of the following data:

1. A class of objects $\mathcal{O}$ whose members are called the 0-cells of $\mathbb{C}$ (generically upper roman from the beginning of the alphabet);

2. For every $A, A' \in \mathcal{O}$ a set $\text{hom}_{\tau}(A,A')$, called tight arrows (generically lower roman from the beginning of the alphabet);

3. For every $A, B \in \mathcal{O}$ a set $\text{hom}_{\lambda}(A,B)$ called loose arrows (generically lower roman from middle of the alphabet);

4. For every $A \in \mathcal{O}$ a distinguished tight arrow $1_A \in \text{hom}_{\tau}(A,A)$;

5. For every $A \in \mathcal{O}$ a distinguished loose arrow $\id_A \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(A,A)$, also written as just $A$ if convenient;

6. For every $A, A', A'' \in \mathcal{O}$, and every $f \in \text{hom}_{\tau}(A,A')$ and also every $f' \in \text{hom}_{\tau}(A',A'')$, there is a $f' \compt f \in \text{hom}_{\tau}(A,A'')$;

7. For every $A, B, A', B' \in \mathcal{O}$, and every $f \in \text{hom}_{\tau}(A,A'), g \in \text{hom}_{\tau}(B,B')$ and also every $p \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(A,B), p' \in \text{hom}_{\tau}(A',B')$, there is a set
$\sq^{A,B}_{A',B'}(f, g, p, p')$ called witnesses (generically lower greek). For simplicity, we will drop identities as redundant information;


::: {.imagify}
[]: % https://q.uiver.app/#q=WzAsNSxbMCwwLCJYIl0sWzIsMCwiWSJdLFswLDIsIlYiXSxbMiwyLCJXIl0sWzEsMSwiXFxEb3duYXJyb3cgXFxwaGkiXSxbMCwxLCJNIiwwLHsic3R5bGUiOnsiYm9keSI6eyJuYW1lIjoiYmFycmVkIn19fV0sWzAsMiwiZiIsMl0sWzIsMywiTiIsMix7InN0eWxlIjp7ImJvZHkiOnsibmFtZSI6ImJhcnJlZCJ9fX1dLFsxLDMsImciXV0=
\begin{tikzcd}
	V && W \\
	& {\Downarrow \phi} \\
	V' && W'.
	\arrow["M"{inner sep=.8ex}, "\shortmid"{marking}, from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow["f"', from=1-1, to=3-1]
	\arrow["g", from=1-3, to=3-3]
	\arrow["M'"'{inner sep=.8ex}, "\shortmid"{marking}, from=3-1, to=3-3]
\end{tikzcd}
:::


8. For every $A, B \in \mathcal{O}$, and every $p \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(A,B)$ there is a distinguished witness $\upsilon_p \in \sq_{A, B}^{A,B}(p, p)$. 
For simplicity, if $p = \id_A$ for $A \in \mathcal{O}$ then we will write $\upsilon_{id_A}$ as $\upsilon_A$;


::: {.imagify}
[]: %
\begin{tikzcd}
	V && W \\
	& {\Downarrow {\upsilon}_N} \\
	V && W.
	\arrow["N"{inner sep=.8ex}, "\shortmid"{marking}, from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow["1_V"', from=1-1, to=3-1]
	\arrow["1_W", from=1-3, to=3-3]
	\arrow["N"'{inner sep=.8ex}, "\shortmid"{marking}, from=3-1, to=3-3]
\end{tikzcd}
:::


9. For every $A, B, A', B', A'', B'' \in \mathcal{O}$, and every $f \in \text{hom}_{\tau}(A,A'), f' \in \text{hom}_{\tau}(A',A''), g \in \text{hom}_{\tau}(B,B'), g' \in \text{hom}_{\tau}(B',B'')$
and also every $p \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(A,B), p' \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(A',B'), p''\in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(A'',B'')$
as well as every $\varphi \in \sq^{A, B}_{A', B'}(f, g, p, p'), \varphi' \in \sq^{A', B'}_{ A'', B''}(f', g', p', p'')$ there is a
$\varphi' \comptt \varphi \in \sq^{A, B}_{ A'', B''}(f' \compt f, g' \compt g, p, p'')$.


::: {.imagify}
[]: %
\begin{tikzcd}
	V && W \\
	& {\Downarrow \phi} \\
	V' && W'\\
    & {\Downarrow \phi'}\\
    V'' && W''. \\
	\arrow["N"{inner sep=.8ex}, "\shortmid"{marking}, from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow["f", from=1-1, to=3-1]
	\arrow["g", from=1-3, to=3-3]
	\arrow["N'"'{inner sep=.8ex}, "\shortmid"{marking}, from=3-1, to=3-3]
	\arrow["f'", from=3-1, to=5-1]
	\arrow["g'", from=3-3, to=5-3]
	\arrow["N''"'{inner sep=.8ex}, "\shortmid"{marking}, from=5-1, to=5-3]
\end{tikzcd}
:::


$$\leadsto$$


::: {.imagify}
[]: %
\begin{tikzcd}
	V && W \\
	& {\Downarrow \phi \smile \phi'} \\
	V'' && W''.
	\arrow["M"{inner sep=.8ex}, "\shortmid"{marking}, from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow["f \frown f'"', from=1-1, to=3-1]
	\arrow["g \frown g'", from=1-3, to=3-3]
	\arrow["M''"'{inner sep=.8ex}, "\shortmid"{marking}, from=3-1, to=3-3]
\end{tikzcd}
:::


10. For every $A, B, C \in \mathcal{O}$ and every $p \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(A,B), q \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(B,C)$
there is a $q \compl p \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(A,C)$. For simplicity we will write $id_B \compl p$ as $B \compl p$.;

11. For every $A, B, C, A', B', C' \in \mathcal{O}$ and every $f \in \text{hom}_{\tau}(A,A'), g \in \text{hom}_{\tau}(B,B'), h \in \text{hom}_{\tau}(C,C')$
and also every $p \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(A,B), q \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(B,C), p' \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(A',B'), q' \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(B',C')$
as well as every witness $\varphi \in \sq^{A, B}_{A', B'}(f, g, p, p')$ and $\psi \in \sq^{B, C}_{B', C'}(g, h, q, q')$ then there is a witness
$\psi \compll \varphi \in \sq^{B,C}_{B',C'}(f, h, q \compl p, q' \compl p')$.

12. For every $A, B \in \mathcal{O}$ and every $p \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(A,B)$ there is
a witness $\ell_p \in \sq^{A, B}_{A, B}(B \compl p, p)$. The witness is natural in $p$ in the sense that: for every $p' \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(A,B)$ and every
$\varphi \in \sq^{A, B}_{A, B}(p, p')$ we have

$$ \varphi \comptt \ell_p =  \ell_{p'} \comptt (\upsilon_{B} \compll \varphi) .$$

Each $\ell_p$ also comes equipped with a friend $k_p \in \sq^{A, B}_{A, B}(p, B \compl p)$
such that $k_p \comptt \ell_p = \upsilon_{B \compl p}$ and $\ell_p \comptt k_p = \upsilon_{p}$;

13. For every $A, B \in \mathcal{O}$ and every $p \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(A,B)$ there is
a witness $\rho_p \in \sq^{A, B}_{A, B}(p \compl A, p)$. The witness is natural in $p$ in the sense that: for every $p' \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(A,B)$ and every
$\varphi \in \sq^{A, B}_{A, B}(p, p')$ we have

$$\varphi \comptt r_p = r_{p'} \comptt (\varphi \compll \upsilon_A)$$

Each $\rho_p$ comes equipped with a friend $\sigma_p \in \sq^{A, B}_{A, B}(p, p \compl A)$
such that $\rho_p \comptt \sigma_p = \upsilon_p$ and $\sigma_p \comptt \rho_p = \upsilon_{p \compl A}$;

14. For every $A, B, C, D \in \mathcal{O}$ and every $r \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(C,D), q \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(B,C), p \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(A,B)$
there is a witness $a_{r, q, p} \in \sq^{A, D}_{A, D}((r \compl q) \compl p, r \compl (q \compl p))$. This witness is natural in $r, q$ and $p$ simultaneously
meaning that: for every $r' \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(C, D), q' \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(B, C), p' \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(A, B)$ and every
$\psi \in \sq^{C, D}_{C, D}(r, r'), \chi \in \sq^{B, C}_{B, C}(q, q'), \varphi \in \sq^{A, B}_{A, B}(p, p')$ we have

$$a_{r', q, p}\comptt ((\psi \compll \upsilon_{q}) \compll \upsilon_{p})  = (\psi \compll (\upsilon_{q} \compll \upsilon_{p})) \comptt a_{r, q, p}$$

$$a_{r, q', p} \comptt ((\upsilon_{r} \compll \chi) \compll \upsilon_{p}) =  (\upsilon_{r} \compll (\chi \compll \upsilon_{q})) \comptt  a_{r, q, p},$$

$$ a_{r, q, p'} \comptt  ((\upsilon_{r} \compll \upsilon_{q}) \compll \varphi) = (\upsilon_{r} \compll (\upsilon_{q} \compll \varphi)) \comptt a_{r, q, p} $$

Each $a_{r, q, p}$ comes equipped with a friend $b_{r, q, p} \in \sq^{A, D}_{A, D}(r \compl (q \compl p)), (r \compl q) \compl p)$
such that $a_{r,q,p} \comptt b_{r, q, p} = \upsilon_{r \compl (q \compl p)}$ and $b_{r, q, p} \comptt a_{r, q, p} = \upsilon_{(r \compl q) \compl p}$.

This data is required to satisfy the following:

For every $A, A' \in \mathcal{O}$ and every $f \in \text{hom}_{\tau}(A,A')$ we have

$$1_{A'} \compt f = f = f \compt 1_{A};$$

For every $A, B, A', B', A'', B'', A''', B''' \in \mathcal{O}$ and every $p \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(A, B), p' \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(A', B'),
p'' \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(A'', B''), p''' \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(A''', B''')$ and also every $f \in \text{hom}_{\tau}(A, A'), g \in \text{hom}_{\tau}(B,B'),
f' \in \text{hom}_{\tau}(A', A''), g' \in \text{hom}_{\tau}(B',B''), f'' \in \text{hom}_{\tau}(A'', A'''),  g'' \in \text{hom}_{\tau}(B'',B''')$ as well as
$\varphi \in \sq^{A, B}_{A', B'}(f, g, p, p'), \varphi' \in \sq^{A', B'}_{A'', B''}(f', g', p', p''), \varphi'' \in \sq^{A'', B''}_{A''', B'''}(f'', g'', p'', p''')$ we have

$$ f'' \compt (f' \compt f) = (f'' \compt f') \compt f,$$

$$ \varphi'' \comptt (\varphi' \comptt \varphi) = (\varphi'' \comptt \varphi') \comptt \varphi;$$

For every $A, B, A', B' \in \mathcal{O}$ and every $p \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(A, B), p' \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(A',B')$ and also every $f \in \text{hom}_{\tau}(A,A'),
g \in \text{hom}_{\tau}(B,B')$ as well as every witness $\varphi \in \sq^{A, B}_{A', B'}(f, g, p, p')$ we have

$$\varphi \comptt \upsilon_p = \varphi = \upsilon_{p'} \comptt \varphi;$$

For every $A, B, C, D, E \in \mathcal{O}$ and every $s \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(D,E), r \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(C,D), q \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(B, C),
p \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(A, B)$ we have

$$ ( (\upsilon_s \compll a_{r, q, p}) \comptt a_{s, r \compl q, p} ) \comptt (a_{s, r, q} \compll \upsilon_p) = a_{s, r, q \compl p} \comptt  a_{s \compl r, q, p};$$

For every $A, B, C \in \mathcal{O}$ and every $q \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(B, C), p \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(A, B)$ we have

$$ (\upsilon_{p} \compll \ell_q) \comptt a_{q, B, p} = \rho_p \compll \upsilon_{B};$$

For every $A, B, C, A', B', C', A'', B'', C'' \in \mathcal{O}$ and $f \in \homt(A,A'), f' \in \homt(A',A''), g \in \homt(B, B'), g' \in \homt(B',B''), h \in \homt(C,C'), h' \in \homt(C',C'')$ and every
$q \in \homl(B,C), p \in \homl(A,B), q' \in \homl(B',C'), p' \in \homl(A',B'), q'' \in \homl(B'',C''), p'' \in \homl(A'', B'')$ and also every $\varphi \in \sq_{A',B'}^{A,B}(f,g,p,p'), \psi \in \sq_{B',C'}^{B,C}(g,h,q,q'), \varphi' \in \sq_{A'',B''}^{A',B'}(f',g',p', p''), \psi' \in \sq_{B'',C''}^{B',C'}(g',h',q',q'')$ we have

$$(\psi \compll \varphi) \comptt (\psi' \compll \varphi') = (\varphi' \comptt \varphi) \compll (\psi' \comptt \psi).$$

:::

::: {#def-double-category-1-categorically}
## Double category, 1-categorical version

A double category $\mathbb{C}$ is the data of

1. A class $\mathcal{O}$ (generically upper roman from the beginning of the alphabet);

2. A set $\homt(A,B)$ for each $A, B \in \mathcal{O}$ (of tight morphisms, generically lower roman from the beginning of the alphabet);

3. A set $\homl(A,B)$ for each $A, B \in \mathcal{O}$ (of loose morphisms, generically lower roman from the middle of the alphabet);

4. A distinguished tight arrow $1_A \in \homt(A,A)$ and a distinguished loose arrow $\text{id}_A \in \homl(A,A)$ for $A \in \mathcal{O}$;

5. For $f \in \homt(A,B), f' \in \homt(B, C)$ there is $f' \compt f \in \homt(A,C)$ for $A, B, C \in \mathcal{O}$;

6. For $p \in \homl(A, B), q \in \homl(B,C)$ there is $q \compl p \in \homl(A,C)$ for $A, B, C \in \mathcal{O}$;

7. A set $\text{Sq}^{A,B}_{C,D}(f,g,p,p')$ for each $f \in \homt(A,C), g \in \homt(B,D)$ and $p \in \homl(A,B), p' \in \homl(C,D)$ for $A, B, C, D \in \mathcal{O}$ (generically lower case greek). For simplicity, we will drop any identities as redundant information;

8. A distinguished square $\upsilon_p \in \text{Sq}_{A,B}^{A,B}(p,p)$ for each $p \in\homl(A,B)$ and for $A, B \in \mathcal{O}$;

9. For $\phi \in \text{Sq}^{A,B}_{C,D}(f,g,p,p'), \phi' \in \text{Sq}^{C,D}_{E,F}(f',g',p',p'')$ there is $\phi' \comptt \phi \in \text{Sq}^{A,B}_{E,F}(f'\compt f,g' \compt g,p,p'')$ for $A, B, C, D, E, F \in \mathcal{O}$;

10. For $\phi \in \text{Sq}^{A,B}_{C,D}(f,g,p,p'), \psi \in \text{Sq}^{B,E}_{D,F}(g,h,q,q')$ there is $\psi \compll \phi \in \text{Sq}^{A,E}_{C,F}(f,h,q \compl p, q' \compl p')$ for $A, B, C, D, E, F \in \mathcal{O}$;

Satisfying the following relations:

For $A, B, C, D \in \mathcal{O}$ and $f \in \homt(A,B), f' \in \homt(B, C), f'' \in \homt(C,D)$ we have that

$$f \compt 1_A = f = 1_B \compt f$$

and

$$(f'' \compt f') \compt f = f'' \compt (f' \compt f);$$

For every $A, B, C, D \in \mathcal{O}$ and $p \in \homl(A,B), q \in \homl(B, C), r \in \homl(C,D)$ we have that

$$p \compl \text{id}_{A} = p = \text{id}_{B} \compl p$$

and

$$(r \compl q) \compl p = r \compl (q \compl p);$$

For every $A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H \in \mathcal{O}$ and $\phi \in \text{Sq}^{A,B}_{C,D}(f,g,p,p'), \phi' \in \text{Sq}^{C,D}_{E,F}(f',g',p',p''), \phi'' \in \text{Sq}^{E, F}_{G, H}(f'',g'',p'', p''')$ we have that

$$\upsilon_{p'} \comptt \phi = \phi = \phi \comptt \upsilon_{p}$$

and

$$(\phi'' \comptt \phi') \comptt \phi = \phi'' \comptt (\phi' \comptt \phi);$$

For every $A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H \in \mathcal{O}$ and $\phi \in \text{Sq}^{A,B}_{C,D}(f,g,p,p'), \psi \in \text{Sq}^{B,E}_{D,F}(g,h,q,q'), \chi \in \text{Sq}^{E, G}_{F, H}(h,k,r,r')$ we have that

$$(\chi  \compll \psi) \compll \phi = \chi \compll (\psi \compll \phi);$$

For every $A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, K \in \mathcal{O}$ and $\phi \in \text{Sq}^{A,B}_{C,D}(f,g,p,p'), \phi' \in \text{Sq}^{C,D}_{E,F}(f',g',p',p''), \psi \in \text{Sq}^{B, G}_{D, H}(g, h, q, q'), \psi' \in \text{Sq}^{D, H}_{F, K}(g', h', q', q'')$ we have that

$$(\phi' \comptt \phi) \compll (\psi' \comptt \psi) = (\phi' \compll \psi') \comptt (\phi \compll \psi).$$

:::


Let $\mathcal{C}\text{at}$ denote the category which has as objects (small) categories and morphisms as functors between these. 

To produce the following definition we will need to be explicit about what the fibre products are in $\mathcal{C}\text{at}$, namely the strict pullbacks. For three (small) categories $C, D, E$ in $\mathcal{C}\text{at}$ and functors $f: C 
\rightarrow E$, $g: D \rightarrow E$. The strict pullback is denoted $C \times_E D$ and it is small category with an object set consisting

$$\text{ob}(C\times_E D) = \{(c,d) \in \text{ob}(C)\times\text{ob}(D) \ :|: \ f^o(c) = g^o(d) \}$$

and morphisms, for each $(c,d)$ and $(c',d')$

$$(C\times_E D)((c,d),(c',d')) = \{(\varphi, \phi) \in \text{hom}_C(c, c') \times \text{hom}_D(d,d') \ :|: \ f^m(\varphi) = g^m(\phi) \in \text{hom}_E(f^o(c),g^o(d'))\} $$

::: {#def-double-category-internal}

::: {#thm-double-category-equivalent}
## The two 1-categorical definitions are essentially the same

A category object in $\mathcal{C}\text{at}$ is equivalently a double category.

A double category is equivalently a category object internal to $\mathcal{C}\text{at}$.

:::

::: {#prf-double-category-equivalent}

$(``\Rightarrow")$

This is a series of definition re-writing.

$$\mathcal{O} \triangleq \text{ob}(C_0)$$

$$\forall A,B \in \mathcal{O}, \ \text{hom}_{\tau}(A,B) \triangleq C_0(A,B)$$

$$\forall A,B \in \mathcal{O}, \ \text{hom}_{\lambda}(A,B) \triangleq \{p \in \text{ob}(C_1) \ :|: \ s^o(p) = A, t^o(p) = B \}$$

$$\forall A \in \mathcal{O}, 1_A \triangleq \text{id}^{C_0}_A$$

$$\forall A \in \mathcal{O}, \text{id}_A \triangleq \text{id}^o(A)$$

$$\forall A, B, C, D \in \mathcal{O}, \forall f \in \text{hom}_{\tau}(A,C), g \in \text{hom}_{\tau}(B,D), p \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(A,B),
 p' \in \text{hom}_{\lambda}(C,D)$$
$$ \text{Sq}_{A,B,C,D}(f,g,p,p') \triangleq
 \{\varphi \in C_1(p,q) \ :|: \ s^o(p) = A, t^o(p) = B, s^m(\varphi) = f, s^o(q) = C, t^o(q) = D, t^m(\varphi) = g\}$$

$$\forall A, B \in \mathcal{O}, \forall p \in \homl (A,B), \upsilon_p \triangleq \text{id}^{C_1}_p$$

$$\forall A, B, C \in \mathcal{O}, \forall f \in \homt(A,B), f' \in \homt(B,C),$$
$$ f'\compt f \triangleq \circ^{C_0}(f',f)$$

$$\forall A, B, C \in \mathcal{O}, \forall p \in \homl(A,B), q \in \homl(B,C),$$
$$ q\compl p \triangleq \ \text{comp}^o((q,p))$$

$$\forall A, B, C, D, E, F \in \mathcal{O}, \forall \varphi \in \sq_{A,B,C,D}(f,g,p,q), \varphi' \in \sq_{C,D,E,F}(f',g',q,r),$$
 $$ \varphi' \comptt \varphi \triangleq \circ^{C^1}(\varphi',\varphi)$$

$$\forall A, B, C, D, E, F \in \mathcal{O}, \forall \varphi \in \sq_{A,B,C,D}(f,g,p,q), \psi \in \sq_{B,E,D,F}(g,h,p',q'),$$
$$ \psi \compll \varphi \triangleq \ \text{comp}^m((\psi, \varphi))$$

$(``\Leftarrow")$

In the other direction.

$$\text{ob}(C_0) \triangleq \mathcal{O}$$

$$\text{Mor}(C_0) \triangleq \{(A,B, f) \ :|: \ f \in \homt(A,B)\}$$

$$\text{id}^{C_0}_A \triangleq (A, A, 1_A)$$

$$\circ^{C_0}((B,C,f'),(A,B,f)) \triangleq (A,C, f' \compt f)$$

$$\ob(C_1) \triangleq \{(A,B, p) \ :|: \ p \in \homl(A,B)\}$$

$$\mor(C_1) \triangleq \{(A,B,p,C,D,q,f,g,\varphi) \ :|: \ \varphi \in \sq_{A,B,C,D}(f,g,p,q)\}$$

$$\text{id}^{C_1}_{(A,B,p)} \triangleq (A,B,p,A,B,p,1_A,1_B, \upsilon_p)$$

$$\circ^{C_1}(((A,B,p,C,D,q,f,g,\varphi),((C,D,q,E,F,r,f',g',\varphi')) \triangleq$$ 
$$ (A,B,p,E,F,r,f'\compt f, g'\compt g, \varphi'\comptt \varphi)$$

Define functors

$$s,t : C_1 \rightarrow C_0$$

by $s^o((A,B,p)) \triangleq A$ and $s^m((A,B,p,C,D,q,f,g,\varphi)) \triangleq (A,C,f)$.

Similarly, $t^o((A,B,p)) \triangleq B$ and $t^m((A,B,p,C,D,q,f,g,\varphi)) = (B,D,g)$.

Also define

$$\text{id} : C_0 \rightarrow C_1$$

by $\text{id}^o(A) \triangleq (A,A,\text{id}_A)$ and $\text{id}^m((A,B,f)) \triangleq (A,A,\text{id}_A,B,B,\text{id}_B,f,f,=).$

Finally define

$$\text{comp} : C_1 \times_{C_0} C_1 \rightarrow C_1$$

by $\text{comp}^o((B,C,q),(A,B,p)) \triangleq (A,C, q \compl p)$ and $\text{comp}^m((B,E,q, D, F, q', g,h,\psi),(A,B,p,C,D,p',f,g,\varphi)) \triangleq$

$$(A,E, q \compl p, C, F, q' \compl p', f, h, \psi \compll \varphi).$$

:::

Whenever we talk of a double category we will mean the definition which starts with a class of objects and two hom-sets, as above.

::: {#exm-1-double-category-rel}
## The double category Rel

We will now describe $\rel$ the double category of relations and functions. Firstly, $\mathcal{O}$ is class of small sets then for sets $A,B$ we define
$\homt(A,B) \triangleq \text{hom}_{Set}(A,B)$ is set of all functions from $A$ to $B$ 
whereas $\homl(A,B)$ is the set of relations $A$ to $B$ viewed as monomorphisms into $A\times B$. The tight composition is simply composition of functions, while loose composition
is defined as composition of relations. The squares are unique if they exist, and are witnessed to exist by the truth of the following logical formula

$$\forall (x,y) \in R \quad : \quad (f(x),g(y)) \in R'. $$   

Where $A, B, A', B'$ are sets, $f : A \rightarrow A', g: B \rightarrow B'$ are functions and $R: A \not\rightarrow B, R' : A' \not\rightarrow B'$ are relations. Tight composition
of cells is the composition of functions while loose composition of cells is the composition of relations which are easily proven to exist by checking the truthfulness of the witness. 
The identity functions are the tight identities, $1_A : A \rightarrow A$ is $x \mapsto x$ and the loose identities is the diagonal relation, $\text{id}_A = \Delta_A \subset A\times A$.
The identity cells $\upsilon_A$ are witnessed by the tautology $(x,y) \in R \Rightarrow (x,y) \in R$. 

:::

::: {#exm-2-double-category-interlaced-bilattices}
## The double category IntBil

Next we will give a description of a double category inspired by multivalued logics. This will use the following [see @Fitting20, Proposition 7.1]

::: {#def-double-functors-1-categorically}
## Double functors, 1-categorical version

Let $\mathbb{C}, \mathbb{D}$ be double categories. A double functor $F:\mathbb{C} \rightarrow \mathbb{D}$ is the data of:

1. For every $A \in \mathcal{O}^C$, then $F^o(A) \in \mathcal{O}^D$;

2. For every $A, A' \in \mathcal{O}^C$ and $f \in \homt^C(A,A')$, then $F^{\tau}(f) \in \homt^D(F^o(A),F^o(A'))$;

3. For every $A, B \in \mathcal{O}^D$ and $p \in \homl^C(A,B)$, then $F^{\lambda}(p) \in \homl^C(F^o(A), F^o(B))$;

4. For every $A, B, A', B' \in \mathcal{O}^C$ and every $f \in \homt^C(A,A'), g \in \homt^C(B,B')$ also every $p \in \homl^C(A,B), p' \in \homl^C(A',B')$ 
as well as $\varphi \in \sq_{A,B,A',B'}(f,g,p,p')$ then $F^{\sq}(\varphi) \in \sq_{F^o(A),F^o(B), F^o(A'), F^o(B')}(F^{\tau}(f),F^{\tau}(g),F^{\lambda}(p),F^{\lambda}(p')).$

Satisfying the following relations

1. $F^{\tau}(f' \compt^C f) = F^{\tau}(f') \compt^D F^{\tau}(f)$; 

2. $F^{\lambda}(q \compl^C p) = F^{\lambda}(q) \compl^D F^{\lambda}(p)$;  

3. $F^{\sq}(\psi {\compll}^C \varphi) = F^{\sq}(\psi) {\compll}^D F^{\sq}(\varphi)$;

4. $F^{\sq}(\varphi' {\comptt}^C \varphi) = F^{\sq}(\varphi') {\comptt}^D F^{\sq}(\varphi)$. 

:::

# Bilattices

:::{#def-bilattice}
## Bilattice

A Bilattice is a non-empty set $\mathbf{B}$ with *four* distinct constants $\mathbf{t}, \mathbf{f}, \bot, \top$ as well as *four* idempotent, associative and commutative binary operators $\land, \lor, \otimes, \oplus$ which further satisfy, for every $a, b \in \mathbf{B}$, absorbative conditions:

1. $a\land(b\lor a) = a;$

2. $a\lor(b\land a) = a;$

3. $a\otimes(b\oplus a) = a;$

4. $a\oplus(b\otimes a) = a.$

Finally, $\mathbf{t}$ is the identity for $\land$ (respectively, $\mathbf{f}$ for $\lor$, $\top$ for $\otimes$, $\bot$ for $\oplus$).
:::

:::{#def-bilattice-morphism}
A set function $\varphi : (\mathbf{B},\land, \lor, \otimes, \oplus, \mathbf{t}, \mathbf{f}, \top, \bot) \rightarrow (\mathbf{B}^{\gimel}, \land^{\gimel}, \lor^{\gimel}, \otimes^{\gimel}, \oplus^{\gimel}, \mathbf{t}^{\gimel}, \mathbf{f}^{\gimel}, \top^{\gimel}, \bot^{\gimel})$ is called a bilattice morphism when it preserves each constant:

1. $\varphi(\mathbf{t}) = \mathbf{t}^{\gimel};$ $\varphi(\mathbf{f}) = \mathbf{f}^{\gimel};$ $\varphi(\top) = \top^{\gimel};$ $\varphi(\bot) = \bot^{\gimel};$

and each operator, for every $a, b \in \mathbf{B}$:

2. $\varphi(a \land b) = \varphi(a) \land^{\gimel} \varphi(b)$;

3. $\varphi(a \lor b) = \varphi(a) \lor^{\gimel} \varphi(b)$;

4. $\varphi(a \otimes b) = \varphi(a) \otimes^{\gimel} \varphi(b)$;

5. $\varphi(a \oplus b) = \varphi(a) \oplus^{\gimel} \varphi(b)$.

:::

:::{#def-interlaced-bilattice}
## Interlaced Bilattice

A Bilattice $(\mathbf{B}, \land, \lor, \otimes, \oplus, \mathbf{t}, \mathbf{f}, \top, \bot)$ is called interlaced if the following two conditions are satisfied:

1. for every $a,b \in \mathbf{B}$ such that $a \land b = a$, and for all $c \in \mathbf{B}$:

$$ (a\otimes c) \land (b \otimes c) = a \otimes c, \quad \text{and} \quad (a\oplus c)\land (b \oplus c) = a \oplus c;$$

2. for every $d,e \in \mathbf{B}$ such that $d \otimes e = d$, and for all $f \in \mathbf{B}$:

$$ (d \land f)\otimes (e \land f) = d \land f, \quad \text{and} \quad (d\lor f)\otimes (e \lor f) = d \lor f.$$

:::

For simplicity, we will from now on supress the extra data and simply write $\mathbf{B}$ for the bilattice as a whole.

:::{#prp-interlaced-bilattice-morphisms}
## Bilattice morphisms preserve interlacing

Whenever $\varphi: \mathbf{B} \rightarrow \mathbf{B}^{\gimel}$ is a bilattice morphism which is also bijective as a set function and further $\mathbf{B}$ is an interlaced bilattice then $\mathbf{B}^{\gimel}$ is also an interlaced bilattice. 

:::




Given two categories $\mathcal{C}$ and $\mathcal{D}$ which have, respectively, products and coproducts the twisted product produces a pair
of categories with the same class of objects, simply the product of the classes of objects $\text{ob}(\mathcal{C})\times \text{ob}(\mathcal{D})$.
The tight category with non-decorated arrows is the product $\mathcal{C} \times \mathcal{D}^{op}$ and the loose category with decorated arrows 
is the product $\mathcal{C} \times \mathcal{D}$.

We will need to define products and coproducts for each category. The first of these, the product in the tight category
$(A_1,A_2)\bowtie (B_1,B_2) \triangleq (A_1 \sqcap_{\mathcal{C}} B_1, A_2 \sqcup_{\mathcal{D}} B_2)$. A prior there is no reason why this should
be a functor, even given functors $\ltimes (B_1, B_2)$ and
 $(A_1,A_2) \rtimes : \mathcal{C} \times \mathcal{D} \rightarrow \mathcal{C}\times\mathcal{D}$ for fixed $(A_1,A_2), (B_1,B_2)$ that coincide
still does mean that the coincidence becomes a functor. What is needed is the interchange law! We call the above situation a Binoidal category (see @Levy03 Appendix A, @power97 Section 3, @roman22 Section 2).
We now ask not the interchange law to hold but for the centre of a Binoidal category, defined as the wide subcategory of morphisms which are central. For our specific case we say $f:(A_1,A_2) \not\rightarrow (B_1, B_2)$ is central when for each $g : (C_1,C_2) \not\rightarrow (D_1,D_2)$;

$$(f \bowtie \text{id}_{(C_1,C_2)}) ; (\text{id}_{(B_1,B_2)} \bowtie g) = (\text{id}_{(C_1,C_2)}\bowtie g) ; (f \bowtie \text{id}_{(D_1,D_2)})$$
and
$$(\text{id}_{(C_1,C_2)} \bowtie f) ; (g \bowtie \text{id}_{(B_1, B_2)}) = (g \bowtie \text{id}_{(A_1,A_2)}) ; (\text{id}_{(D_1,D_2)} \bowtie f).$$

Essentially, this unravels to be asking that each component of $f = (f_1, f_2)$, $f_1 : A_1 \rightarrow B_1$, $f_2 : A_2 \rightarrow B_2$ is central. Which is guaranteed by the universal property of the product, and coproduct, respectively.

A Premonoidal category is a Binoidal category with coherence morphisms being central. A useful fact is that the centre of a premonoidal category is monoidal. Therefore, a premonoidal category equivalent to its own centre is immediately monoidal.

-->

# Preorder Categories

## Starting Definitions

::: {#def-Preorder-Categories}
## Pseudo Category object in the thin 2-category PreOrd

\bigskip

A Preorder Category $\mathbb{C}$ is the data of:

- A class sized preorder $\mathcal{O}$ with relation symbol ($\sqleq$), whose elements are called the objects of $\mathbb{C}$;

- For each pair  of objects $x,y$ there is a set $\homl(x,y)$ whose elements are called loose arrows e.g. $f: x \not\rightarrow y$;

- For each object $x$ a distinguished loose arrow in $\homl(x,x)$ written $\id_x : x \not\rightarrow x$;

- For each triple of objects $x, y, z$ and loose arrows $f: x \larr y$, $g : y \larr z$ there is a loose arrow $g \circ f: x \larr z$;

- For each quadruple of objects $x' \sqleq x$, $y' \sqleq y$ and loose arrows $f: x \larr y$, $f': x' \larr y'$ there is at most one arrow 
from $f$ to $f'$ written $f' \sqleq f$;

- For each pair of objects $x,y$ and loose arrow $f : x \larr y$ then $f \sqleq f$;

- For each pair of objects $x' \sqleq x$ then $\id_{x'} \sqleq \id_x$;

- For each pair of objects $x, y$ and loose arrow $f: x \larr y$, then 

$$f \circ \id_x \sqleq f \sqleq f \circ \id_x \quad \text{and} \quad \id_y \circ f \sqleq f \sqleq \id_y \circ f;$$ 

- For each quadruple of objects $x, y, z, w$ and loose arrows $f: x \larr y$, $g : y \larr z$, $h : z \larr w$, then

$$(h \circ g) \circ f \sqleq h \circ (g \circ f) \sqleq (h \circ g) \circ f;$$

- For each hextuple of objects  $x'' \sqleq x' \sqleq x$, $y'' \sqleq y' \sqleq y$ and loose arrows $f : x \larr y$, $f' : x' \larr y'$, 
$f'' : x'' \larr y''$ with $f' \sqleq f$ and $f'' \sqleq f'$ then $f'' \sqleq f$;

- For each hextuple of objects $x' \sqleq x$, $y' \sqleq y$, $z' \sqleq z$ and loose arrows $f: x \larr y$, $g: y \larr z$, $f': x' \larr y'$,
$g' : y' \larr z'$ such that $f' \sqleq f$ and $g' \sqleq g$ then $g' \circ f' \sqleq g \circ f$.


:::

::: {#rem-simplified-notation}
# Simplified Notation

\bigskip

For the sake convenience it is useful to introduce the notation:

$$x \simeq x' \quad \iff \quad x' \sqleq x \sqleq x'$$

on objects in a preorder category and 

$$ f \simeq f' \quad \iff \quad f' \sqleq f \sqleq f'$$

on loose arrows, read as $x$ is equivalent to $x'$ and $f$ is equivalent to $f'$.

Then in the definition above we would replace with

$$f \circ \id_x \simeq f \quad \text{and} \quad \id_y \circ f \simeq f$$

as well as

$$(h \circ g) \circ f \simeq h \circ (g \circ f).$$

:::

::: {#def-Preorder-oplax-functors}
## Preorder oplax functors between preorder categories#

\bigskip

Let $\mathbb{C}$ and $\mathbb{C}^{\gimel}$ be two preorder categories a preorder oplax functor between them, written
$F :  \mathbb{C} \rightarrow \mathbb{C}^{\gimel}$, is the data of:

- An order preserving function $F^{\text{o}} : \mathcal{O} \rightarrow \mathcal{O}^{\gimel}$;

- For each pair of objects $x, y \in \mathcal{O}$ and loose arrow $f : x \larr y$ there is a loose arrow 
$F^{\lambda}_{x, y}(f): F^{\text{o}}x \larr F^{\text{o}}y$;

- For each quadruple of objects $x' \sqleq x$, $y' \sqleq y$ and loose arrows $f: x \larr y$, $f': x' \larr y'$ such that $f' \sqleq f$ then 

$$F^{\lambda}_{x',y'}(f') \sqleq^{\gimel} F^{\lambda}_{x,y}(f);$$

- For each object $x \in \mathcal{O}$ then 

$$\id^{\gimel}_x \sqleq^{\gimel} F^{\lambda}_{x,x}(\id_x);$$

- For each triple of objects $x, y, z \in \mathcal{O}$ and loose arrows $f: x \larr y$, $g: y \larr z$ then 

$$F^{\lambda}_{y,z}(g) \circ^{\gimel} F^{\lambda}_{x,y}(f) \sqleq^{\gimel} F^{\lambda}_{x,z}(g \circ f).$$

:::

::: {#rem-preorder-pseudofunctor}
## Preorder Pseudofunctor

\bigskip

We would have the definition of a preorder psuedofunctor by tweaking the above definition in the following way: (we replace with)

$$F^{\lambda}_{x',y'}(f') \simeq^{\gimel} F^{\lambda}_{x,y}(f),$$

$$\id^{\gimel}_{F^{\text{o}}x} \simeq^{\gimel} F^{\lambda}_{x,x}(\id_x),$$

$$\text{and} \quad F^{\lambda}_{y,z}(g) \circ^{\gimel} F^{\lambda}_{x,y}(f) \simeq^{\gimel} F^{\lambda}_{x,z}(g \circ f).$$

:::

::: {#rem-composition-of-preorder-pseudofunctors}
## Composition of Preorder Pseudofunctors

\bigskip

Given three preorder categories $\mbbc$, $\mbbc^{\gimel}$, $\mbbc^{\beth}$ and preorder psuedofunctors $F : \mbbc \rightarrow \mbbc^{\gimel}$,
$G: \mbbc^{\gimel} \rightarrow \mbbc^{\beth}$ then define their composition

- The underlying order preserving function $(G\circ F)^{\text{o}} \triangleq G^{\text{o}}\circ F^{\text{o}} : \mathcal{O} \rightarrow \mathcal{O}^{\beth}$;

- For each pair of objects $x,y \in \mathcal{O}$ and loose arrow $f: x \larr y$ then define

$$(G \circ F)^{\lambda}_{x,y}(f) \triangleq G^{\lambda}_{F^{\text{o}}x,F^{\text{o}}y}(F^{\lambda}_{x,y}(f)) : G^{\text{o}}(F^{\text{o}}x) \larr G^{\text{o}}(F^{\text{o}}y).$$

:::

::: {#def-sqleq-transformations}
## Comparing two preorder pseudofunctors through the order

\bigskip

Given preorder categories $\mbbc$, $\mbbc^{\gimel}$ as well as a pair of preorder pseudofunctors $F :\mbbc \rightarrow \mbbc^{\gimel}$, 
$G: \mbbc \rightarrow \mbbc^{\gimel}$ then a $\sqleq$-transformation from $F$ to $G$, written $G \sqleq F$, are the following assertions

- For each object $x \in \mathcal{O}$, $G^{\text{o}}x \sqleq^{\gimel} F^{\text{o}}x$;

- For each pair of objects $x, y \in \mathcal{O}$ and $f : x \larr y$ then $G^{\lambda}_{x,y}(f) \sqleq^{\gimel} F^{\lambda}_{x,y}(f)$. 

:::

::: {#def-loose-transformations}
## Comparing two preorder pseudofunctors loosely

\bigskip

Given preorder categories $\mbbc$, $\mbbc^{\gimel}$ as well as a pair of preorder pseudofunctors $F :\mbbc \rightarrow \mbbc^{\gimel}$, 
$G: \mbbc \rightarrow \mbbc^{\gimel}$ then a loose transformation from $F$ to $G$, written $\alpha : F \larr G$, is the following data

- For each object $x \in \mathcal{O}$ a loose arrow $\alpha_x : F^{\text{o}}x \larr G^{\text{o}}x$;

- For each pair of objects $x' \sqleq x$ in $\mathcal{O}$ then $\alpha_{x'} \sqleq \alpha_x$.

This data is required to satisfy:

- For each pair of objects $x, y$ in $\mathcal{O}$ and loose arrow $f : x \larr y$ 

$$\alpha_y \circ^{\gimel} F^{\lambda}_{x,y}(f) \simeq G^{\lambda}_{x,y}(f) \circ^{\gimel} \alpha_x.$$

:::

::: {#def-modifications}
## Comparing loose transformations 

\bigskip

Given preorder categories $\mbbc$, $\mbbc^{\gimel}$ and a quadruple of preorder pseudofunctors $H \sqleq F : \mbbc \rightarrow \mbbc^{\gimel}$,
$K \sqleq G : \mbbc \rightarrow \mbbc^{\gimel}$ and loose transformations $\alpha : F \larr G$, $\beta : H \larr K$ then there is modification
from $\alpha$ to $\beta$, written $\beta \sqleq \alpha$, when for each object $x \in \mathcal{O}$ we have that $\beta_x \sqleq \alpha_x$.

:::

::: {#def-product-preorder-category}
## Products of Preorder Categories

\bigskip

Given a pair of preorder categories $\mbbc$ and $\mbbc^{\gimel}$ we can form a new preorder category which is their product,
$\mbbc \times \mbbc^{\gimel}$, consisting of the data:

- The class $\mathcal{O}^{\times} \triangleq \mathcal{O}\times\mathcal{O}^{\gimel}$ with the componentisewise order;

- For each pair, of pairs, of objects $(x_1,x_2)$ and $(y_1,y_2)$ the set 

$$\homl^{\times}((x_1,x_2),(y_1,y_2)) \triangleq \homl(x_1,x_2) \times \homl^{\gimel}(y_1,y_2);$$

- For each object $(x_1,x_2)$ a distinguised loose arrow $\id^{\times}_{(x_1,x_2)} \triangleq (\id_{x_1}, \id^{\gimel}_{x_2})$;

- For each triple $(x_1,x_2), (y_1,y_2), (z_1,z_2)$ and loose arrows $(f_1,f_2) : (x_1,x_2) \larr (y_1,y_2), (g_1,g_2) : (y_1,y_2) \larr (z_1,z_2)$
there is a loose arrow

$$(g_1,g_2) \circ^{\times} (f_1,f_2) \triangleq (g_1 \circ f_1, g_2 \circ^{\gimel} f_2) : (x_1,x_2) \larr (z_1,z_2);$$

- For each quadruple $(x_1',x_2') \sqleq^{\times} (x_1,x_2), (y_1',y_2') \sqleq^{\times} (y_1,y_2)$ and loose arrows $(f_1,f_2): (x_1,x_2) \larr (y_1,y_2), (f_1', f_2') : (x_1',x_2') \larr (y_1',y_2')$ there is an arrow

$$(f_1', f_2') \sqleq^{\times} (f_1, f_2)  \iff \quad f_1' \sqleq f_1 \quad \land \quad f_2' \sqleq^{\gimel} f_2.$$

:::

::: {#thm-product-preorder-category}
## The product of preorder categories is a preorder category

\bigskip

This is a simple checking that the definitions given above are enough to conclude the rest of the assertions.

For example, given objects $(x_1,x_2), (y_1,y_2)$ and a loose arrow $(f_1,f_2) : (x_1,x_2) \larr (y_1,y_2)$ then we have that 
$(f_1,f_2) \sqleq^{\times} (f_1,f_2)$ as we have that both $f_1 \sqleq f_1$ and $f_2 \sqleq^{\gimel} f_2$ hold. 

:::

::: {#def-2-category-preorder-categories}
## The thin 2-category of preorder categories

\bigskip

Let $\pspreordcat$ denote the monoidal (thin) 2-category with: 

- 0-cells: Preorder categories $(\mathbb{C}, \mathbb{C}^{\gimel}, \mathbb{C}^{\beth}, \mathbb{D},...)$;

- 1-cells: Preorder pseudofunctors $(F: \mathbb{C} \rightarrow \mathbb{C}^{\gimel}, G : \mathbb{C}^{\gimel} \rightarrow \mathbb{C}^{\beth},...)$;

- 2-cells: $\sqleq$-transformations between preorder pseudofunctors ($G \sqleq F : \mathbb{C} \rightarrow \mathbb{C}^{\gimel}$).

and monoidal product the product of preorder categories defined above.

:::

::: {#def-monoidal-preorder-category}
## Monoidal Preorder Category

\bigskip

A monoidal preorder category is a preorder category $\mbbc$ with a distinguished object $1 \in \mathcal{O}$ with a loose arrow $\nu : 1 \larr 1$
and an assignment:

- For each pair of objects $x_1,x_2$ an object $x_1 \otimes x_2$;

- For each quadruple of objects $x_1, x_2, y_1, y_2$ and loose arrows $f_1 : x_1 \larr y_1$, $f_2 : x_2 \larr y_2$ a loose arrow
$f_1 \otimes f_2 : x_1 \otimes x_2 \larr y_1 \otimes y_2$.

This assignment must satisfy the following properties:

- For each quadruple $x_1' \sqleq x_1$, $x_2' \sqleq x_2$ then $x_1'\otimes x_2' \sqleq x_1 \otimes x_2$;

- For each octuple $x_1' \sqleq x_1$, $x_2' \sqleq x_2$, $y_1' \sqleq y_1$, $y_2' \sqleq y_2$ and quadruple of loose arrows
$f_1' : x_1' \larr y_1'$, $f_2' : x_2' \larr y_2'$, $f_1 : x_1 \larr y_1$, $f_2 : x_2 \larr y_2$ such that $f_1' \simeq f_1$ and
$f_2' \simeq f_2$ then 

$$f_1' \otimes f_2' \simeq f_1 \otimes f_2;$$ 

- For each pair of objects $x_1, x_2$  then $\id_{x_1 \otimes x_2} \simeq \id_{x_1} \otimes \id_{x_2};$

- For each hextuple $x_1, x_2, y_1, y_2, z_1, z_2$ and quadruple of loose arrows $f_1 : x_1 \larr y_1$, $f_2 : x_2 \larr y_2$,
$g_1 : y_1 \larr z_1$, $g_2 : y_2 \larr z_2$ then 

$$(g_1 \otimes g_2) \circ (f_1 \otimes f_2) \simeq (g_1 \circ f_1) \otimes (g_2 \circ f_2);$$

- For each hextuple $x_1, x_2, x_3, y_1, y_2, y_3$ and loose arrows $f_1 : x_1 \larr y_1$, $f_2 : x_2 \larr y_2$, $f_3: x_3 \larr y_3$ then

$$(x_1 \otimes x_2) \otimes x_3 \simeq x_1 \otimes (x_2 \otimes x_3)$$

$$ \text{and} \quad (f_1 \otimes f_2) \otimes f_3 \simeq f_1 \otimes (f_2 \otimes f_3);$$

The assignment interacts with the distinguished object through $\nu \simeq \id_{1}$ and

- For each object $x$, $1 \otimes x \simeq x$ and $x \otimes 1 \simeq x$. 

:::

::: {#def-exponentiating-by-small-preorder-categories}
## Exponential Preorder Category

\bigskip

Given $\mbbx$ a (small) preorder category and $\mbbc$ some other preorder category. 

- Consider the class

$$\mclo^{\text{ps}} \triangleq \pspreordcat(\mbbx, \mbbc)$$

of all preorder pseudofunctors from $\mbbx$ to $\mbbc$ these will be the objects of the proposed exponential $(\mbbc^{\mbbx})$, with the preorder
exactly given by $\sqleq$-transformations;

- For each pair of preorder pseudofunctors $F : \mbbx \rightarrow \mbbc, G : \mbbx \rightarrow \mbbc$ there is a set $\homl^{\text{ps}}(F,G)$
which are $\alpha : F \larr G$ loose transformations; 

- For each $F : \mbbx \rightarrow \mbbc$ there is $\id_F : F \larr F$ with components for each $x \in \mclo^{\mbbx}$,
$(\id_F)_x \triangleq \id_{F^\text{o}x}^{\mbbc}$;

- For each triple $F : \mbbx \rightarrow \mbbc, G : \mbbx \rightarrow \mbbc, H : \mbbx \rightarrow \mbbc$ and loose transformations 
$\alpha : F \larr G, \beta : G \larr H$ then there is a loose transformation with components for each $x \in \mclo^{\mbbx}$, 
$(\beta \circ \alpha)_x \triangleq \beta_x \circ^{\mbbc} \alpha_x$;

- For each quadruple $F' \sqleq F, G' \sqleq G$ and loose transformations $\alpha: F \larr G, \alpha': F' \larr G'$ then there is at most 
modification from $\alpha$ to $\alpha'$ written $\alpha' \sqleq \alpha$;

:::

::: {#thm-exponentiating-by-small-preorder-categories-gives-a-preorder-category}
## Exponentiating-by-small-preorder-categories-gives-a-new-preorder-category

\bigskip

Once again we simply need to check the data defined above is sufficient. 

For example, if we have a pair of preorder pseudofunctors with $G \sqleq F : \mbbx \rightarrow \mbbc$, then for each $x \in \mclo^{\mbbx}$, 
$G^{\text{o}}x \sqleq^{\mbbc} F^{\text{o}}x$ and so $\id_{G^{\text{o}}x}^{\mbbc} \sqleq^{\mbbc} \id_{F^{\text{o}}x}^{\mbbc}$, which implies 
$\id_{G} \sqleq \id_F$. 

:::

::: {#def-preorder-psuedo-endofunctors-of-small-preorder-categories-are-monoidal-preorder-categories}
## Preorder Psuedo Endofunctors form a monoidal Preorder Categories

\bigskip

Let $\mbbx$ be a small Preorder Category. We wish to put a monoidal structure on $\mbbx^{\mbbx}$. To begin define the assignment on objects and loose arrows: 

- For each pair $F_1 : \mbbx \rightarrow \mbbx, F_2 : \mbbx \rightarrow \mbbx$ then define 
$F_1 \otimes F_2 \triangleq F_2 \circ F_1 : \mbbx \rightarrow \mbbx$;

- For each quadruple $F_1, F_2, G_1, G_2 : \mbbx \rightarrow \mbbx$ and a pair of loose transformatiomns $\alpha : F_1 \larr G_1$, 
$\beta : F_2 \larr G_2$ then there is a loose transformation $\alpha \otimes \beta : F_1 \otimes F_2 \larr G_1 \otimes G_2$. 
Which has components, for each $x \in \mclo^{\mbbx}$, defined as

$$(\alpha \otimes \beta)_x \triangleq \beta_{G_1^{\text{o}} x} \circ^{\mbbx} (F_2)^{\lambda}_{F^{\text{o}}_1 x, G^{\text{o}}_1 x}(\alpha_x);$$

Also define the unit as $\id_{\mbbx}$ the identity pseudo preorder functor on $\mbbx$ and $\nu : \id_{\mbbx} \larr \id_{\mbbx}$, which for each $x \in \mclo^{\mbbx}$ is defined componentwise $\nu_x = \id_{x}$.

:::

::: {#lem-the-componentwise-definition-in-fact-defines-a-loose-transformation}
## Verify the assignment on loose transformations does produce a loose transformation

\bigskip

- For each pair of objects $x' \sqleq x$ in $\mclo^{\mbbx}$ we have as $G_1^{\text{o}}x' \sqleq G_1^{\text{o}}x$ and by $\beta$ being a loose transformation

$$\beta_{G_1^{\text{o}}x'} \sqleq \beta_{G_1^{\text{o}}x}.$$

Furthermore, $\alpha_{x'} \sqleq \alpha_x$ as $\alpha$ is a loose transformation, thus

$$(F_2)^{\lambda}_{F_1^{\text{o}}x', G_1^{\text{o}}x'}(\alpha_{x'}) \sqleq (F_2)^{\lambda}_{F_1^{\text{o}}x, G_1^{\text{o}}x}(\alpha_{x}).$$

Finally, gauranteed by $\mbbx$ being a preorder category we have

$$(\alpha \otimes \beta)_{x'} = \beta_{G_1^{\text{o}}x'}\circ^{\mbbx} (F_2)^{\lambda}_{F_1^{\text{o}}x', G_1^{\text{o}}x'}(\alpha_{x'}) \sqleq  \beta_{G_1^{\text{o}}x}\circ^{\mbbx} (F_2)^{\lambda}_{F_1^{\text{o}}x, G_1^{\text{o}}x}(\alpha_{x}) = (\beta \otimes \alpha)_x.$$

- Given a pair of objects $x,y \in \mclo^{\mbbx}$ and loose arrow $f : x \larr y$ then 

$$(\alpha \otimes \beta)_y \circ (F_1 \otimes F_2)^{\lambda}_{x,y}(f)$$

$$= (\beta_{G_1^{\text{o}} y} \circ^{\mbbx} (F_2)^{\lambda}_{F^{\text{o}}_1 y, G^{\text{o}}_1 y}(\alpha_y)) \circ^{\mbbx} (F_1 \otimes F_2)^{\lambda}_{x,y}(f)$$

$$\simeq \beta_{G_1^{\text{o}} y} \circ^{\mbbx} ((F_2)^{\lambda}_{F^{\text{o}}_1 y, G^{\text{o}}_1 y}(\alpha_y)) \circ^{\mbbx} (F_1 \otimes F_2)^{\lambda}_{x,y}(f))$$

$$= \beta_{G_1^{\text{o}} y} \circ^{\mbbx} ((F_2)^{\lambda}_{F^{\text{o}}_1 y, G^{\text{o}}_1 y}(\alpha_y) \circ^{\mbbx} (F_2)^{\lambda}_{F_1^{\text{o}}x,F_1^{\text{o}}y}((F_1)^{\lambda}_{x,y}(f))) $$

$$ \simeq \beta_{G_1^{\text{o}}y} \circ^{\mbbx} (F_2)^{\lambda}_{F^{\text{o}}_1 x, G^{\text{o}}_1 y}(\alpha_y \circ^{\mbbx} (F_1)^{\lambda}_{x,y}(f))$$

$$ \simeq \beta_{G_1^{\text{o}}y} \circ^{\mbbx} (F_2)^{\lambda}_{F^{\text{o}}_1 x, G^{\text{o}}_1 y}((G_1)^{\lambda}_{x,y}(f) \circ^{\mbbx} \alpha_x)$$

$$ \simeq \beta_{G_1^{\text{o}}y} \circ^{\mbbx} ((F_2)^{\lambda}_{G^{\text{o}}_1 x, G^{\text{o}}_1 y}((G_1)^{\lambda}_{x,y}(f)) \circ^{\mbbx} (F_2)^{\lambda}_{F^{\text{o}}_1 x, G^{\text{o}}_1 x}(\alpha_x))$$

$$ \simeq (\beta_{G_1^{\text{o}}y} \circ^{\mbbx} (F_2)^{\lambda}_{G^{\text{o}}_1 x, G^{\text{o}}_1 y}((G_1)^{\lambda}_{x,y}(f))) \circ^{\mbbx} (F_2)^{\lambda}_{F^{\text{o}}_1 x, G^{\text{o}}_1 x}(\alpha_x)$$

$$ \simeq ((G_2)^{\lambda}_{G^{\text{o}}_1 x, G^{\text{o}}_1 y}((G_1)^{\lambda}_{x,y}(f)) \circ^{\mbbx} \beta_{G_1^{\text{o}}x}) \circ^{\mbbx} (F_2)^{\lambda}_{F^{\text{o}}_1 x, G^{\text{o}}_1 x}(\alpha_x)$$

$$ \simeq (G_2)^{\lambda}_{G^{\text{o}}_1 x, G^{\text{o}}_1 y}((G_1)^{\lambda}_{x,y}(f)) \circ^{\mbbx}( \beta_{G_1^{\text{o}}x} \circ^{\mbbx} (F_2)^{\lambda}_{F^{\text{o}}_1 x, G^{\text{o}}_1 x}(\alpha_x))$$

$$ = (G_2)^{\lambda}_{G^{\text{o}}_1 x, G^{\text{o}}_1 y}((G_1)^{\lambda}_{x,y}(f)) \circ^{\mbbx} (\alpha \otimes \beta)_x$$

$$ = (G_1 \otimes G_2)_x \circ^{\mbbx} (\alpha \otimes \beta)_x$$


:::



<!---

::: {#rem-preorders-are-square-less-than-preorder-categories}
## The 2-category of (small) preorders is a sub-2-category of preorder categories

\bigskip

Any Preorder may be viewed as a preorder category where the sets of loose arrows are empty, there is a 2-functor that establishes this 
relationship.


:::

# MSP 201

## Topos Theory

Meeting 05/10/26 

We started with the definition of subobject classifier given in Definition 1.1 of @Leinster10

:::{#def-Subobject-Classifier}
## Subobject Classifier

Let $\mathcal{E}$ be category with a terminal object, $1$. A subobject classifier in $\mathcal{E}$ is an object $\Omega$ and an arrow $t : 1 \rightarrow \Omega$ out of the terminal object satisfying the 
following condition: Given any monomorphism $m : A \hookrightarrow X$ there exists a unique morphism $\chi: X \rightarrow \Omega$ such that the following square is a pullback.

::: {.imagify}
[]: %
\begin{tikzcd}
	A && 1 \\
	&  \\
	X && \Omega.
	\arrow["!_A", from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow["m"', hook, from=1-1, to=3-1]
	\arrow["t", from=1-3, to=3-3]
	\arrow["\chi"', from=3-1, to=3-3]
\end{tikzcd}
:::

:::


Checking our intuition first we began with showing that $\Omega = \{0,1\}$ with $t : 1 = \{\star\} \rightarrow \Omega$ mapping to $1$ is indeed the subobject classifier. The repeated situation that 
occured again and again is that there are neccessary choices for $\chi$ by the commutativity of square (this assumes we are working in a concrete category which is reasonable for our examples).
Then the uniqueness occurs when considering the pullback condition. 

We next consider the category $\mathcal{S}\text{et}^{B\mathbb{N}}$ which can be instead thought of as the category of dynamical systems, this means nothing more than a set with 
a self map called the update function. These dynamical systems can viewed through little pictures, $\mathcal{D}\text{yn}\mathcal{S}\text{ym}$ is equivalently $\Omega(1)$ the 
category of unary algebras. The morphisms of this category are then graph homomorphism, equivalently unary algebra homomorphisms, furthermore the monomorphisms are simply 
injective unary algebra homorphisms. This is a clearly a very nice category to work with for intuition. 

We now looked at trying to write down what the subobject classifier is for unary algebras. The first pass intuition was to consider the graph of natural numbers with $0$ as a sink
and arrows decrementing by 1. Other attempts included the graph of natural numbers with successor. This lead us to think about adding a place of absolute untruth as somewhere 
inaccessible from anywhere else. We then asked why we couldn't simply have the discrete graph on 2 points. Finally thinking about a game between 2 players one trying to find the 
correct subobject classifier and the other trying to break with continued counterexamples produced the original first pass but we also realised that we needed to reintroduce the
place of untruth from before. The final answer is summarised below.

::: {.imagify}
[]: %
\begin{tikzcd}
	\cdots & 2 & 1 & 0 \\
	&& \bot
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow[from=1-2, to=1-3]
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=1-4]
	\arrow[from=1-4, to=1-4, loop, in=55, out=125, distance=10mm]
	\arrow[from=2-3, to=2-3, loop, in=305, out=235, distance=10mm]
\end{tikzcd}
:::

Sieves are the oidification of right ideals for monoids. By viewing $\Omega(1)$ as presheaves on the delooping of $\mathbb{N}$ we can just consider right ideals of the natural
numbers under addition. The formula for the subobject classifier for presheaf categories gives us exactly the same as above with 0 standing for $\mathbb{N}$, 1 for
$\mathbb{N}\setminus\{0\}$, 2  for $\mathbb{N} \setminus \{0, 1\}$ and so on... until $\bot$ is exactly empty.
